# A conditional centroid bound in terms of effective fiber count

This is a proved conditional bound for the actual mixed-volume centroid.
It does not give the conjectured factor for arbitrarily many effective
fibers. It applies to all ambient cap orientations.

## Statement

Let d>=1 and let C be a convex body in R^n x R^d. Write

    K_z={x:(z,x) in C},     a_z=vol_d(K_z),
    M=sum_(z in Z^n) a_z>0.

Let g=(z0,x0) be the centroid of this mixed-volume measure, and assume
z0 is integer. Then g belongs to C intersect (Z^n x R^d). For every closed
ambient halfspace H containing g,

    vol_d(K_z0 intersect H_z0)
       >= gamma_d [sum_z a_z^(1+1/d)/M]^d.               (1)

Only the mass in the centroid fiber occurs on the left. In particular

    depth_S(g)>=gamma_d/N_eff,
    N_eff=M^(d+1)/[sum_z a_z^(1+1/d)]^d.                 (2)

If N_eff<=2^n, this proves the exact desired conditional centroid bound
2^(-n) gamma_d. The condition holds whenever there are at most 2^n
positive-volume fibers. Zero-volume fibers do not affect the statement.

## 1. Concavity of cap-volume roots

Fix u in R^d and v in R^n and put

    F(z,t)=vol_d{x in K_z: u.x+v.z>=t},
    G(z,t)=F(z,t)^(1/d).

Whenever two cap fibers have positive volume, convexity gives

 lambda {x in K_z:u.x+v.z>=t}
 +(1-lambda){x in K_w:u.x+v.w>=s}
   subset {x in K_(lambda z+(1-lambda)w):
               u.x+v.(lambda z+(1-lambda)w)
                       >=lambda t+(1-lambda)s}.

Ordinary d-dimensional Brunn--Minkowski therefore proves concavity of G
on its positive domain. That domain is convex. The same inequality holds
when one of the nonempty cap fibers has zero volume, with its root set to
zero. All relevant cap fibers are bounded by one common compact set.

The function F is upper semicontinuous in (z,t): if parameters converge,
any compact subset of the complement of the limiting cap fiber is
ultimately disjoint from the approximating cap fibers. Thus their limsup
sets lie in the limiting cap fiber, and continuity from above for bounded
neighborhoods bounds limsup of their volumes by the limiting volume.
The root G is likewise upper semicontinuous. These facts justify Jensen's
inequality also when the mean lies on the boundary of the positive domain.
For an explicit formulation, approximate any bounded probability law
supported there by finite laws with their means converging and their
G-expectations converging; finite concavity followed by upper
semicontinuity gives G(mean)>=E G.

## 2. The exact conditional expectation

Suppose u!=0. For a positive fiber K_z, let X_z be uniform on K_z and set
T_z=u.X_z+v.z. The distribution of T_z is continuous, since hyperplanes
have d-dimensional volume zero. Its survival function is F(z,t)/a_z.
The probability integral transform gives

    F(z,T_z)/a_z uniform on [0,1].

For completeness, the projection of a positive convex body has an interval
as its support, and every interior subinterval has positive projected
measure. Thus its continuous distribution function is strictly increasing
on the support interior, so the usual inverse-function verification of
the transform applies directly. Consequently

    E[G(z,T_z)]=a_z^(1/d) integral_0^1 s^(1/d)ds
              =[d/(d+1)] a_z^(1/d).                     (3)

Equivalently the unnormalized integral is
[d/(d+1)] a_z^(1+1/d).

## 3. Jensen at the actual mixed centroid

It suffices to treat a halfspace through g, since every containing closed
halfspace contains its parallel halfspace through g. Write such a cap as

    H={u.x+v.z>=u.x0+v.z0}.

Draw (Z,X) from normalized mixed volume. Its mean is g. The mean of
(Z,u.X+v.Z) is (z0,u.x0+v.z0). Applying Section 1 and then (3) gives

    G(z0,u.x0+v.z0)
       >=E G(Z,u.X+v.Z)
       =[d/(d+1)] sum_z a_z^(1+1/d)/M.

Raising to the dth power proves (1). The ordinary centroid g belongs to
C because it is a probability barycenter of points of the compact convex
set C; the integer-base hypothesis therefore makes it a single point of
S itself. No rounding is used.

If u=0, the cap contains the entire centroid fiber. In this case apply
Jensen directly to the concave root a(z)^(1/d) of the ordinary continuous
fiber-volume function. It gives

    a_z0^(1/d)>=sum_z a_z^(1+1/d)/M.

This is stronger than (1). Vertical closed boundaries, which can carry a
whole fiber's mass, are thus covered separately without discarding them.

## 4. Effective count and the exact range covered

If N is the number of positive fibers, Holder gives

    sum_z a_z^(1+1/d)>=M^(1+1/d)/N^(1/d),

so 1<=N_eff<=N. More precisely, (1) implies the exact OC factor whenever

    sum_z a_z^(1+1/d)>=2^(-n/d) M^(1+1/d).

Long products with many equal-volume fibers show that integer centroid
membership does not by itself force this effective-count condition. For
example, symmetric consecutive integer fibers of equal positive volume
have an integer centroid and N_eff=N. A proof for those remaining cases
must use cap mass in fibers other than z0; (1) alone does not supply it.

When n=0 there is one fiber and (1) is precisely the ordinary sharp
Grunbaum bound at the centroid. The argument requires d>=1; it makes no
claim concerning the separate purely discrete d=0 conditional problem.

## 5. A complete halfspace case split for three consecutive fibers

Suppose n=1 and exactly the three positive fibers at -1,0,1 occur. If the
mixed centroid has integer base 0, the endpoint volumes are equal, say a,
and write b for the middle volume. Brunn--Minkowski gives b>=a. Let m be
the continuous midpoint of the two endpoint centroids, and let c be the
middle centroid. Then the actual continuous centroid is

    x0=(2a m+b c)/(2a+b).

For any chosen cap through (0,x0), let L be its affine defining functional,
positive on the included side. Evaluate the endpoint average by

    L_m=[L(-1,g_-)+L(1,g_+)]/2=L(0,m).

If L_m>=0, at least one endpoint centroid belongs to the cap, so its
contribution is at least gamma_d a by ordinary Grunbaum. The centroid-fiber
bound (1) is at least gamma_d b/2. To check the latter put r=b/a>=1. If
1<=r<=2, its volume factor

    [(2+r^(1+1/d))/(2+r)]^d

is at least 1>=r/2. For r>=2 (in fact for every r>=1), weighted
arithmetic-geometric mean gives

    (2+r^(1+1/d))/(2+r) >= r^[r/(d(r+2))].

Its dth power divided by r is therefore at least r^[-2/(r+2)], which
is at least 1/2. Here is an explicit verification of the last elementary
inequality. The function

    h(r)=(r+2)log(2)-2log(r)

is strictly convex on r>0 and has its minimum at r=2/log(2), where
h=2[1+log(log(2))]>0. Indeed 1/2<log(2)<1, by integrating 1/t on
[1,2], so log(log(2))>log(1/2)=-log(2)>-1. Thus
2log(r)<(r+2)log(2), as required.

The whole cap consequently has mass at least gamma_d(a+b/2), exactly
gamma_d M/2. The weighted-AMGM argument is valid in every d>=1; no
linear-in-d simplification of the root expression is used.

If L_m<0, the centroid identity forces L(0,c)>0. Hence the middle cap
alone has mass at least gamma_d b. This proves the same target whenever
b>=2a.

Consequently a possible failure for three consecutive positive fibers
must involve a cap with L_m<0 and a<=b<2a. This is only an exact reduction
of that restricted conditional-centroid problem, not a proof in this
remaining regime or for longer fiber families.
